mentions.story: MIT lecturer Ana Bell discusses books to learn CS and programming
mentions.text:
So first of all let me preface my own list of books with the following: These book recommendations are for some books that are really really good IMO but this list of books alone is far from all that you need. You need practice. Lots and lots of practice. You need interesting problems to work on that are sufficiently small in scope that they don't each take too much time, but which still end up teaching you something. You need to know when to skip a problem if you're banging your head and getting nowhere, and you need to know when to persist. So the following should not be taken as a list that will "teach you CS and/or programming", but rather a list of books to complement learning.

mentions.author: rayalez
mentions.story: How to learn Deep Learning in 6 months
mentions.text:
Good post. I want to add several great resources.

- Grokking Deep Learning

[link]

This is a fantastic book that assumes no prerequisites other than knowing python, and takes you through the fundamentals of DL. It has very intuitive and easy to follow explanations, and doesn't use any libraries other than NumPy, so you're building the whole thing yourself, from scratch.

- Deep Learning With Python

[link]

This is kind of the opposite of the previous one, it doesn't go into math and theory, instead it guides you through building several practical projects with a very simple to use DL library(keras). It's a great way to gain practical experience in addition to theory from the previous…

mentions.author: FourierT-form
mentions.text:
I would start with vectors and physics.

Note that there is some basic calculus involved in both of those.

The Wikipedia is a bit dense, but if you take the time to follow links to concepts that you aren't familiar with you should be good.

[link]

You might have done a little bit of calculus with High School trig without knowing it. Sometimes Trig is mixed in with Analysis for some nuanced reasons.

I would check out the Khan academy post for a basic grounding in calculus.
